abstract: Abstract Purpose Epidemiological studies have reported that environmental factors from fetal period to early childhood can influence the risk of non-communicable diseases in adulthood. This concept has been termed the developmental origins of health and disease (DOHaD). The Chiba study of Mother and Child Health (C-MACH) is a DOHaD concept-based birth cohort study which started in 2014. This study aims to investigate the effects of genetic and environmental factors, particularly fetal and postnatal living environment, on children’s health. We also aim to identify candidate biomarkers for their health status. Moreover, the second phase study of C-MACH which was initiated in 2021 aimed at expanding the sample size, especially for gut microbiota and epigenomic analysis; it also aimed at clarifying the impact of the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic on children’s health. Participants This study consists of four hospital-based cohorts. Women who were <13 weeks pregnant and their partners were enrolled in the study. All data and biological samples will be stored in the Chiba University Centre for Preventive Medical Sciences. Findings to date A total of 561 women and their partners provided their consent to participate in this study. Of these women, 505 completed the questionnaire during the early gestational period. The mean age of the 505 women at enrolment was 33.0 (SD, 4.5) years. The mean prepregnancy body mass index (BMI) was 21.7 (SD, 3.6) kg/m 2 , with 74.5% of the women having a BMI of 18.5–24.9 kg/m 2 . About 5.2% of the women smoked cigarettes during the early stages of pregnancy. Future plans The primary study outcomes are allergies, obesity, endocrine and metabolic disorders and developmental difficulties in children. Variables related to genome, metabolome, epigenome, gut microbiota and exposome will be evaluated as health-related factors. The relationships between these outcomes and the health-related factors will be analysed.
body:
STRENGTHS AND LIMITATIONS OF THIS STUDY
The Chiba study of Mother and Child Health collected a diverse array of biomaterials from mother–child pairs, including maternal and child blood, urine, faeces, breast milk, deciduous teeth, umbilical cords, umbilical cord artery, umbilical cord blood and paternal saliva samples.
Intrauterine exposure factors are evaluated by the maternal lifestyle, nutritional status, levels of environmental chemicals in maternal bio-samples, children’s deciduous teeth, indoor air and house dust.
Several analytical methods, including genomic analysis, epigenomic analysis, gut microbiota and metabolomics, will be combined to explore the health effects of various environmental factors on child health later in life. Children will be followed to observe health effects such as allergies, non-communicable diseases and developmental difficulties.
This study is a hospital-based cohort. Thus, participants may not be representative of the rest of the Japanese population.
The study sample size is relatively small to determine the impact of fetal environmental factors on all child’s health problems. However, it will provide a basis for future research on the developmental origin of health and disease concept. In addition, we will combine the first and second phase studies, as appropriate.
Introduction
Along with the recent rapid changes in the environment and lifestyle, the number of patients with allergic diseases, metabolic diseases and mental disorders is increasing. Recently, epidemiological studies, mainly in Europe, have pointed out the possibility that the nutritional environment since the fetal period to infancy may influence the risk of developing metabolic diseases in adulthood,
1
3
and the concept of developmental origins of health and disease (DOHaD) was proposed.
1 4
Subsequently, many studies have been reported to support this concept; it is now widely accepted that the risk of various chronic diseases is increased by the addition of postnatal environmental factors to prenatal environmental factors including maternal nutritional status, lifestyle, stress and exposure to environmental pollutants during the fetal period.
5
This DOHaD phenomenon mechanism assumes that epigenetic changes in genes, which are changes in the regulatory mechanism of gene expression that do not involve changes in the genomic DNA base sequence, are induced by exposure to environmental factors during fetal life. More recently, the idea that imbalances in the gut microbiota affect not only digestive diseases but also the development of systemic diseases has become widespread.
6
Mothers and children are also exposed to a wide variety of chemicals in the environment, and there is concern about the health effects associated with such exposure. However, insufficient progress has been made in monitoring new environmental chemicals such as new per- and polyfluoroalkyl compounds (PFAS), pesticides and plasticisers, unverified volatile organic compounds (VOCs) and unknown compounds that are not subject to regulation. In this study, we will reveal the effects of these chemicals.
The effects of environmental factors during the fetal period and right after birth on child growth, development and health have become a global issue; therefore, nationwide and international collaborative research is essential. For example, in Japan, several birth cohorts have formed the Japan birth cohort consortium (JBiCC).
7
The birth cohort consortium of Asia (BiCCA), a consortium of birth cohort studies mainly focusing on Asia, is conducting research and identifying situations unique to Asia.
8
Our birth cohort will also participate in JBiCC and BiCCA. These collaborations will contribute to child health and preventive medicine not only in Japan but also in the whole world.
Chiba City serves a multifaceted role as the centre of Chiba Prefecture, located just east of Tokyo, and is part of the Greater Tokyo Area. Many workers and their families reside in Chiba, contributing to a population of approximately 1 million. The city combines both urban and suburban characteristics, with a blend of developed areas and abundant natural surroundings. Its relatively high rates of maternal and child healthcare utilisation make it an ideal setting for studying the health and developmental trajectories of mothers and children. Furthermore, the region’s access to high-quality medical facilities and established research infrastructure supports robust data collection and longitudinal follow-up. Additionally, the laboratory at Chiba University processes umbilical cords and cord blood, enabling the separation of mononuclear cells and cord arteries for detailed analysis. To facilitate the processing of fresh, non-frozen samples, we limited the distance for sample collection to areas near Chiba University. For these reasons, we selected Chiba City as the location for this cohort study.
This study aims to reveal how genetic and environmental factors, particularly the prenatal and postnatal living environments, influence child’s health. A total of 433 mothers participated in the first phase of the Chiba study of Mother and Child Health (C-MACH)
9
which started in February 2014, and the study is still ongoing. Moreover, in the second phase of the study, which has begun in 2021, we aim to expand the sample size, especially for gut microbiota and epigenomic analysis, and clarify the impact of the recent coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic on health indicators, lifestyle, and environment of children, and lifestyle changes of the mothers, in addition to the objectives of the first phase. We will assess whether the changes in environmental factors due to COVID-19 pandemic, such as sterilisation, use of masks, avoidance of contact with others, and COVID-19 infection itself influence changes in the gut microbiota and overall health of the mothers and children.
Cohort description
Inclusion and exclusion criteria
The study-related information was disseminated through bulletin boards in the hospitals/clinics and on the website (
http://cpms.chiba-u.jp/kids/
). Women who were <13 weeks pregnant and their partners were enrolled at three cooperating hospitals/clinics in Chiba, Japan. Women who had miscarriage or stillbirth events or were transferred to another hospital or clinic that was not cooperating with the study for any reason were excluded from participation in this cohort. The pregnant women who were transferred from the three cooperating hospitals or clinics to Chiba University Hospital continued the study.
All children born to the participating women were enrolled as study participants. If a woman withdraws herself from participation, her child or children and her partner will also be withdrawn.
Sample size
The target sample size was 500 pregnant women. The prevalence of obesity among children in Japan is about 10%.
10
Based on the obesity outcome, the study was designed to have 90% power to detect a difference of 1 kg/m
2
in BMI
10
between the low- and high-exposure groups. This resulted in an estimated sample size of approximately 380 participants. In addition, the prevalence of developmental difficulties, including mild disabilities, is about 8%–9%. The Japanese version of the Ages and Stages Questionnaires, Third Edition (J-ASQ-3), was also used to screen for the risk of developmental disabilities. The study was designed with 90% power to detect a 0.5-point difference between the high- and low-exposure groups. As a result, the estimated sample size was approximately 330 participants. The sample size allows us to assess the effects of the fetal environment on health problems such as obesity and developmental difficulties. Owing to the long study duration, some participants may drop out.
In other cohort studies of mothers and children, the dropout rate by age 12 was about 30%, and a similar dropout rate is expected for this cohort. Therefore, a larger sample size (>30% more) was targeted. Moreover, integrating data from the first phase of the C-MACH study will compensate for the shortfall. The selected sample size is enough and allows us to assess whether the fetal environment has an effect on long-term health problems including obesity. The statistical programme R (V.3.2.0;
http://cran.ism.ac.jp
; R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria) was used to estimate the sample sizes.
Multivariate analysis will be conducted to explore the biomarkers and indicators of epigenetics and metabolomic changes related to the children’s health problems. A sample size of several hundred participants is needed to obtain statistically valid results. Moreover, gut microbiota analysis required several hundred participants; thus, we are collecting faeces samples from 500 pairs of mothers and children. In the first phase study, faeces samples of 100 pairs were collected. Therefore, we will combine the first and second phase studies to obtain a sufficient sample size in this field.
Recruitment
Recruitment began in June 2021 and ended in April 2023. The study included only women who were scheduled to deliver at the participating hospitals or clinics.
A research coordinator, doctor, nurse or midwife at each hospital provided written and oral explanations for the participants. Written consent was obtained from the pregnant women and their partners. Participating mothers gave consent as a proxy for their children. Since most of the participants in Japan are Japanese citizens, there were no language-related barriers. Thus, the documents, including the information sheet, were described in Japanese.
Consent to participate in the second phase C-MACH was obtained from 561 women. A total of 48 women withdrew after providing informed consent, five miscarriages and three spontaneous stillbirths, resulting in a final cohort of 505 women (figure 1).
Figure 1
Flow diagram of the study participants Consent to participate was obtained from 561 women. A total of 48 women withdrew, five miscarriages and three spontaneous stillbirths, resulting in a final cohort of 505 women.
Follow-up program
The study duration is currently defined as lasting until participants reach 15 years of age. Therefore, all participants are going to be followed up until every child grows up to be 15 years old. The follow-up schedule is shown in
online supplemental table 1
. Self-administered questionnaires were administered twice to mothers and once to fathers during pregnancy. The questionnaire surveys include lifestyle habits, socioeconomic status, psychological evaluation, chemical sensitivity and a Brief-type Self-administered Diet History Questionnaire.
11
Transcripts of data of routine medical check-ups conducted during pregnancy were collected until delivery. During the first and last trimesters of pregnancy, peripheral blood, urine and faecal samples will be collected from pregnant women to analyse for the presence of environmental chemicals, hormones, immunoglobulin (Ig)E and cytokines.
Records of childbirth were collected. Umbilical cord blood and umbilical cord are going to be collected from the Miyake, Onodera and Kaihin Cohorts. Breast milk samples were collected 1 and 4 months after delivery.
Peripheral blood samples are going to be collected from children at 3.5 years of age. Invasive examinations for children including blood sampling will be minimised in order not to burden them.
Strategies for retaining study participants include providing partial individual examination results, newsletters with study findings, seasonal greeting letters and rewards for returning questionnaires as feedback to participants.
Outcome measurements
The primary outcomes of this study include allergies, developmental difficulties, endocrine and metabolic disorders and obesity in children. The questionnaires will be used to obtain these data. Data on perinatal complications and birth size were collected by medical record transcripts. The allergic status in children will be assessed according to the diagnosis of the physicians, medical questionnaire of the international study of asthma and allergies in childhood, and serum IgE levels against several allergens. Health check-up records, medical history, and developmental milestones by J-ASQ-3
12
will be collected using a questionnaire which will be completed by the parents. BMI will be calculated using the height and weight measurements of the children retrieved from the follow-up data to assess obesity in children. Children-related information will be collected from questionnaires completed by parents at the ages of 1, 4 and 10 months, 1.5, 3.5 and 5 years. For the developmental milestones, J-ASQ-3 will be administrated at 1.5, 3.5 and 5 years of age.
Multiomics analyses
Genomic, epigenomic, gut microbiota variables, metabolomic and humoral factors are planned to be analysed (
table 1
) to identify the useful biomarkers. These results will be synthesised and examined in conjunction with the environmental factors and children’s health outcomes.

Genomic analysis is going to be performed on cord blood, maternal blood and paternal saliva samples. DNA is going to be extracted from these samples, and genome-wide association analysis using single-nucleotide polymorphisms is going to be conducted to evaluate the impact of the genome on outcomes such as allergy, metabolic diseases and epigenome.
For the epigenetic analysis, DNA methylation is proposed as one of the mechanisms of epigenetics in the DOHaD model.
13
Therefore, microarrays, bisulfite sequencing and methylation-sensitive high-resolution melting analysis will be used to perform comprehensive epigenetic analysis and investigate DNA methylation in the fetal tissues.
14
DNA extracted from the faecal samples collected from mothers and their children will be used for carrying out gut microbiota analysis. The distribution and bias of gut microbiota will be examined through the acquisition of 16S rRNA sequence data.
15
20
In this study, non-targeted metabolomics using liquid chromatography-quadrupole time-of-flight mass spectrometry will be performed to analyse the environmental chemicals and metabolites. This approach aims to simultaneously assess the exposure composition and its effects. By employing both octadecyl and hydrophobic columns, a broad spectrum of metabolomics, including hydrophilic and hydrophobic compounds and lipids, will be screened and analysed. This analysis will be conducted in relation to the outcomes such as obesity and developmental disorders. We will incorporate internal standards and use quality control samples in our analysis to ensure accuracy and establish a framework for semiquantitative comparisons. Exposure assessment
Questionnaires are administered to gather data about parents’ education, income, occupation, smoking habits including passive smoking and alcohol consumption during pregnancy. Comprehensive measurements of environmental chemicals, including known substances such as pesticides and PFAS, and residues in biological and environmental samples will be used to estimate the combined exposure effects.
Combining non-targeted high-resolution mass spectrometry with conventional targeted analysis of chemicals such as PFAS, neonicotinoids, and VOCs may enable the comprehensive monitoring of substances detectable by gas chromatography-mass spectrometer and liquid chromatography-mass spectrometer, even in the absence of reference materials, and above their detection limits. Moreover, indoor dust samples are collected to measure the environmental chemicals and allergens, such as house dust mites, fungi and foods, to assess the indoor environmental effects.
Covariates, mediators and potential confounders
Lifestyle, nutritional habits, physical environment and socioeconomic status obtained from questionnaires will also be investigated as covariates, mediators and confounders. Biochemical examination and hormone-level measurements will be performed using maternal blood and umbilical cord blood. The levels of cholesterol, glycoalbumin, and some vitamins will be measured using maternal blood during the first and third trimester of pregnancy, and umbilical cord blood (
box 1
).
Statistical analysis
We will analyse the association between health status assessment items and biospecimen analysis data, measurement data and medical information/questionnaire items that may be risk factors. This will also include associations with epigenomic alterations, genetic polymorphisms, gut microbiome profiles and metabolomic alterations in blood, urine, faeces, umbilical cord, umbilical cord blood and placenta.
Data will be reported as mean±SD. Bivariate analyses will be conducted to clarify the correlation between dependent variables, such as BMI, J-ASQ-3 and serum IgE levels, and independent variables. Moreover, we will employ a hierarchical Bayesian model, L1 and L2 regularisation, and other analytical methods. Statistical significance will be defined as p<0.05 for all analyses. Microarray or microbiome data will also be analysed using false discovery rates.
Data management system and biospecimen storage
The data will be stored in the database at the Chiba University Centre for Preventive Medical Sciences (CPMS). Blood, umbilical cord blood, umbilical cord, breast milk and faeces samples will be stored at −80°C in the CPMS BioBank in Chiba University until measurement. Cord blood cells are stored in liquid nitrogen with cell storage reagent.
Ethics
The study protocol was approved by the Biomedical Research Ethics Committee of the Graduate School of Medicine, Chiba University (ID 451: first application date 8 November 2013; ID 1239: latest application date 29 March 2023). Regarding genome analysis, the protocol has been approved for blood metabolome analysis, comprehensive genomic and epigenomic analysis, and RNA analysis. The initial approval date was 21 April 2022. The latest approval date is 2 August 2024.
Patient and public involvement
Patient and public involvement is essential for the development of C-MACH, emphasising its dedication to inclusiveness and collaborative research. The integration of patient and public involvement guarantees active engagement of the public in shaping the research project.
Findings to date
The general sociodemographic characteristics of Japan in 2022 are presented for non-participants. The percentage of miscarriages in Japan in 2022
21
was 1.97%, while the percentage of spontaneous stillbirths was 0.94%. In contrast, among the participants in the second phase of the C-MACH cohort, the percentage of miscarriages was 0.97% (5/513, including total births, miscarriages and spontaneous stillbirths), and the percentage of spontaneous stillbirths was 0.58% (3/513). Therefore, the percentages of miscarriages and spontaneous stillbirths in the second phase of C-MACH are lower than those of non-participants. The number of withdrawals before delivery was 48 cases, and these withdrawals were not counted as participants.
The actual cohort population consists of 505 women and their 504 partners who responded to the early pregnancy questionnaire. For the umbilical cord epigenome study, umbilical cords were collected for 478 women; thus, they are candidates of the study. For the gut microbiota analysis, the 461 women who were able to collect faeces samples during early gestation are candidates for the gut microbiota analysis.
Of the 505 women, 5.4% were <25 years old, 24.6% were 25–29 years old, 38.8% were 30–34 years old and 31.3% were ≥35 years old. The mean age was 33.0 (SD, 4.5) years. The percentage of women expecting their first child was 36.8%. The mean age of women expecting their first child was higher than that of the Japanese population data in 2019 (31.8 (SD, 4.8) vs 30.7 years, respectively).

Strengths and limitations
One of the strengths of this study is the combination of a variety of analyses, including multiomics analyses, making it possible to analyse the effects of the various factors on children. This study’s findings will form the basis for future research concerning the DOHaD concept, as in the case of other large-scale birth-cohort studies. This study is expected to provide novel information for research in the fields of genomics, epigenomics, metagenomics and metabolomics.
This study will comprehensively assess the intrauterine environmental factors by evaluating the effects of pollutant exposure, gut microbiota and the external environment on the fetus, in addition to variables related to maternal lifestyle, nutrition and blood biochemistry.
Moreover, the second phase study aims to expand the sample size, especially gut microbiota and epigenomic analysis, and clarify the impact of the recent COVID-19 pandemic on health indicators.
This is a prospective cohort study designed to collect data on various environmental factors, including in utero exposure to chemicals. Detailed data are needed to detect the potential effects of fetal and neonatal environmental factors on childhood outcomes.
There are a few limitations in this study. First, the sample size may not be large enough to determine the effects of prenatal environmental factors on asthma, atopic dermatitis, diabetes and developmental disorders. Second, this study is going to follow the children up until the age of 15 years. Thus, the study duration may not be long enough to fully evaluate the DOHaD concept. Accordingly, although follow-up plans after adolescence have not yet been fleshed out, we are considering continuing follow-up for the children after they turn 15 years of age. Third, this is a hospital-based cohort study; therefore, the participants may not be representatives of the rest of the Japanese population. Additionally, there is an uneven distribution in the participant numbers among the facilities, although it is worth mentioning that these facilities are situated within the same city. Consequently, any observed differences may be relatively minor. Another limitation of this study is the possibility that the participants may change their place of residence. To avoid dropouts, periodic bulletins will be issued and sent to the participants to encourage their continued participation in the study.
The importance of this study is highlighted by the following points, almost no other cohort has analysed the gut microbiota of mothers during pregnancy and that of their children after birth over time on this scale in Japan. While other cohorts use cord blood for epigenomic studies, this study is unique in that it also uses cord tissue and cord arteries for such analyses.
27
Collaboration
The C-MACH is open to future collaborations with external research groups. Researchers can submit proposals for collaborative research to the C-MACH research committee. The research committee will review these proposals and give a decision regarding their adoption. The criteria for review are whether the proposed research protocol: (1) is consistent with the objectives of C-MACH; (2) does not duplicate other research already underway; (3) has funding to proceed and (4) does not harm the cohort participants. Calls for collaborative research proposals from external groups will be initiated after the recruitment phase is completed, basic data set has been reviewed and confirmed, data cleaning has been completed and initial results have been verified.
